chunks.text: But then I haven't got everybody on, have I? Sorry? Haven't got everybody on to do the- Yeah, we need to We're just waiting for the live stream. You're a long way away. I know. Hello. Hello. So, just before we start, one of the reasons for that was we thought that other room, last time there were people standing, and we thought of this as a bigger room. But it just means that we're sort of here to here.

But we do have members coming online as well, so yeah. Great. Right. So, just before we start, I'm just seeking leave. We've got a couple of people from committee members. We've got a couple of people who have asked to take photos, and I'm seeking leave from the committee.

There's one member of the public and one member from Tim's office. Are people okay with that? Good? Yep. That's fine. Thank you. Okay, welcome. Welcome to our hearing here with Fire and Emergency this afternoon. We are starting, and welcome, Ravin. It's your first time in front of our committee, and I'm sorry to hear that your plane got canceled, but it's lovely that we've got the technology for you to come in online.

Thank you very- So, we've got five minutes to start with you, and then we'll open up with all of your opening remarks, and then we'll open from there, according to the structured agenda for questions. So, I'll hand to whoever is going to start with the opening remarks. I will start, Madam Chair. Thank you.

And I do apologize. This is indeed my first appearance and, I very much would have preferred to be there in person. But Fire and Emergency welcomes the opportunity to continue assisting in this inquiry. In the room with yourselves is the Chief Executive and National Commander, Kerry Gregory; Deputy Chief Executive, Megan Stifler; and Chief Financial Officer, Darryl Purdy.

At the previous appearance, Fire and Emergency described the challenge of managing a large, specialized, and nationally dispersed fleet, including continuing pressure around the Type 3 and aerial appliances. Today, I want to acknowledge those challenges, set out what has changed, and what remains to be done.

When I first looked at this issue, I thought, "This must be simple. We're just buying a truck. How hard can it be?" But a fire appliance is not simply a truck. It is a bespoke, complex machine operating in difficult environment. It is clear Fire and Emergency's fleet experience has been affected by procurement and contract management challenges, supplier performance, and COVID disruptions.

Those factors have a very long tail, and that long tail is the reason why we are here. The Type 3 decisions were made in good faith when Fire and Emergency needed to renew an aging fleet and get appliances on the road. But the two-stage chassis and body build approach has not delivered the timeliness, the reliability, or clarity of accountability that was intended.

Would we approach these parts of that program differently now? Definitely. But we must pick the resultant issues up, address them, learn from them, and make the best decisions from here. In my short time as Chair, three weeks, I have raised these matters with the chief executive and have been briefed on the reviews and changes that have already been made.

Our focus will be on stronger contract management, clearer escalation of risks, better fault information reporting, disciplined acceptance processes, and greater board visibility of major programs. For future complex appliance, Fire and Emergency should, where practicable, favor more integrated or turnkey procurement models with clearer accountability for the complete appliance.

That does not mean removing operational input. Firefighters' expertise remain essential in defining requirements, testing suitability, training crews, and confirming readiness. It means applying that input at the right stages with clear decision rights.

I do not want to suggest that all the problems have been solved, because they have not. The legacy tail will continue, and further issues may emerge. Indeed, we have paused the rollout of the Type 3s following discovery of a filter issue in operational testing, which the supplier is now working through.

Like I said, it's not just buying a new truck. The board's responsibility is to ensure the organization responds quickly, applies lessons across the fleet, and provides the oversight required for the aerial program and future procurement. There is also wider funding challenges.

Fire and Emergency responds to a broader range of emergencies these days, while maintaining a specialized heavy fleet. The minister has commissioned a review of the funding mechanism. We will provide evidence about the investment challenge, recognizing that the options available involve difficult choices. Madam Chair, my approach today is straightforward.

We will not minimize the experience of firefighters or communities. We will acknowledge the concerns, be factual about how we arrived here, and be clear about what has changed and what remains to be done. Our focus is stronger procurement, better information, clearer accountability, and sustained governance oversight.

I am reassured that overall, Fire and Emergency continues to respond effectively to emergency events. I want to close by thanking the thousands of career and volunteer firefighters who work together to keep our communities safe, and the people across Fire and Emergency who support them.

Thank you, and we look forward to assisting the committee. Thank you. Thank you very much, Ravin. And we also would've loved to have seen you in person, but next time. And you might notice that we've got some members as well online, for similar reasons as well.

So there's a few of us here and then some online. So I'm just going to say to members online that can you please, if you've got a question, can you please put your virtual hand up and I will be watching that as well. But we're going to start with the first part of the structured agenda, which is the current and future strategy and capital planning. And I think, Tim, you have the first- Thanks... question.

Thanks, Madam Chair. Thank you, Ravin, thanks defense staff who are attending here. I'll just start. Fundamental question, is fleet a strategic priority for FENZ? Yes. Why is it not listed in the national strategy as a strategic priority? If you look at the national strategy, it talks to building stronger business foundations. Fleet is part of those stronger business foundations that we're building for the organization.

Right. So as I try to unpick this and understand it, there's a few documents that sort of cover fleet. There's the asset management plan. Mm-hmm. And then there's a fleet strategy, and then there's the future operating capability. So correct me if I've got this wrong, the fleet strategy is yet to come out. That will go to the, is it next year we're expecting that to go to the board for approval?

Correct. The fleet strategy, itself hasn't been developed yet. And the reason for that is that it's been important for the organization to get a good picture of our assets through the asset management plan. So over the last few years we've been developing the asset management plans, one of those being the fleet asset management plan. And that gives a really defined 10-year journey of how we reduce the age of the fleet to within 90% of it within the target age of that.

So I guess the approach up to this point has been very much a like for like replacement of our assets. But certainly as we move forward, those three things you mentioned, the asset management plans, the future operating capability, and the fleet strategy itself will form the grouping of documents that will help guide us as an organization around the strategy of how we ensure that we're developing the right long-term strategy.

So I understand what you're saying. Is it the right way around, though? If your future operating capability is designed to consider more broadly the service requirements and what it is that it looks like in the future- Mm-hmm... surely you would start from that, then you would build out what your fleet strategy is to enable that, and then you could come up with the asset management plan because the asset management plan, as you say, is like for like.

Mm-hmm. But without those sort of defined and agreed levels of service, we're talking about assets with a 20-year, 20 to 25 lifespan that take a long time to introduce. Mm-hmm. Don't we need to start by looking at 2040, 2050 and starting from that rather than an asset management plan that is built on like for like when we know that like for like probably isn't the answer?

So I think in the initial stages of the organization coming together in 2017 and the legacy of fleet assets that we inherited through there, stabilizing the fleet needs to be the initial focus of that. So you're right in an ideal world, that looking out seems the logical thing to do, but making sure that we can stabilize the fleet first so that we actually can build the rest of the information that needs to build that fleet strategy.

And that's around what's the long-term context and how that's changing, and we've seen lots of changes in the way that we're being asked to deploy into communities. That's looking at a risk-based profile rather than just a like for like across the longer term. And it also looking at things like affordability, and the longer term maintenance costs of all of that asset base.

So it's affordability lens put across that as well. So the fleet, you've described the fleet asset management plan as a deliberate forward-looking roadmap for managing fleet over the next decade. And it clearly distinguishes between what is required and what can be delivered. Mm-hmm. But, and we'll get into type specific stuff further on, but do we actually know, until we define what those sort of service delivery levels are, until we know what the appliances actually need- Mm-hmm we're not forward looking and we're not distinguishing between what is

required and what can be delivered because if you look at the aerial fleet, the asset specifications were not static inputs. In other words, what we were looking for changed as the project went on. So surely we have to start with that capability definition, don't we? Mm-hmm. But I think it's hard in any organization to forecast what the end result's going to be, and it will be an evolving thing as we move forward.

But getting the asset management plans in place and having an understanding around what's the long-term plan to reduce that age of a fleet has been really important to ensure that we're focused in the right places while we build the next book. So there's been a lot of pieces of intelligence or information missing from the organization that's allowed us to bring all that together to actually form a robust strategy. And that is where the future operation capability, the asset plans, now we have a really good picture of that,

come together, which will help us develop, not a simple strategy, but a more mature strategy that sets us up for the future and allows us to look at what are the changing context and how do we make those critical investment decisions and trade-offs as we move to a different way of operating as the context changes around us as an organization.

I guess my fundamental concern is that we sort of have a culture, and it's not just within FENZ and FENZ- Mm... of providing administrative solutions to mechanical problems. We add more layers of paper and things that achieve compliance, and yet we've got an asset management plan, but has it helped? I don't know. I'd argue maybe it hasn't.

We have all these sort of layers and then think, all these bits of paper, are they actually making it any better when you go to the local fire station? And... Well, personally, I think the asset management plans have helped in that there's a real detailed plan around how we bring that age profile of the fleet over the next 10 years. We didn't have that prior to the asset management plans.

So, that gives a really good picture that sits in there. If we look at the development of the FOC work, that's another big piece of work that'll actually look at not just a one-size-fits-all, but looking at what the risk is and how we apply different capabilities to different risk. So, that will inform the asset management plans around the decisions that could be made in there.

So, if you haven't got that work, you need to develop it to make a difference. The difference that people will see on the ground floor, that firefighters will see, and I certainly acknowledge the frustration that our firefighters have. When we've got an aging fleet and they're breaking down at times, that's so frustrating. I've been in the situation myself, so I, in no way, disregard the frustration that our firefighters feel when they have appliances break down. And that's why there's needed to be a focus on how do we

stabilize that first? How do we actually focus on ensuring that the appliances that we're rolling out the door aren't breaking down, we're bringing them with an age profile. And that's not a short-term fix. Like I say, we've got a 10-year plan that's really definitive about that. And just final one if I can, and then so how would, given these things you say they are actually adding value- Mm... how would you assess FENZ is going against your asset management goals?

Say that question again, sorry. How would you assess FENZ is doing against your asset management goals? Oh, against the asset management goals. Well, I think, what we're doing is we're building the foundations to make us successful in the space. If I look at some of the procurements that we've had over the past years, the things like the Type 1s, the Type 2s, they've been really good procurement end-to-end processes. Our Type 3s has just been frustrating for everybody, and taken far longer than anyone would've anticipated that to have take or that's acceptable for that to take.

But it's learning from the different processes and putting those in place so that we are applying what's working well and improving as we move forward. The asset management plans, that's going to stand us in really good stead to actually have confidence that over a 10-year plan, we're going to bring the assets age to that, but we can't do it overnight, and that's the frustration.

Sorry, I meant the specific five asset management goals that you have. How we're going against them? Yes. I'd have to come back to you with the response on that. I don't want to mislead the committee and- No, that's fine. Are you aware of the five asset management goals? Mm-hmm. Can you just give us an example of one of those goals and then how you would assess how you're going?

I can't give them verbatim, but, Daryl, have you got those there? It's in the asset management plan. No. You've got five asset management goals that are listed in your 10-year plan, 2020 to 2030. In the 10-year plan. So in our asset management fleet plan, you're talking about? No, in the FENZ...

Yeah, it'll be up there. I'm not sure which document you're referring to. In your 10-year plan, 2020 to 2030, page 38 will have your asset management goals. Oh, the 10-year plan has been superseded by the strategy. So that's the national strategy, but that's 2019 to 2045.

That starts a year earlier. It's been superseded by the current strategy that takes us through to 2030, so from '25 to 2030. So that was a preexisting document. Right. So does the 2019 to 2045 strategy still, is that still a thing? We only have one organizational strategy, which is the current strategy.

Which is the '25 to '30? Yes. So the one that went out to 2045 is gone? Yes. So the current strategy is only a five-year plan? Yes. And that recognizes the fact that in a five-year continuum, things change. Things are changing really fast and that thing. So having a strategy that goes out to 2045, I would say that no one could predict what 2045 would look like for us as an organization.

But isn't that the point of future operating capability, is to look out to say, because the assets that you buy are going to be operating in 2050 2050 plus. So future operating capability is different from our current strategy, which takes us through to 2030. What we're doing as an organization is, the organization has tried to do too much and hasn't been focused.

So having a clear focus through our strategy for the next five years, or the five years of the time of the strategy, to actually ensure that the organization's focusing on the right things to take us forward. And that is looking at our safe, resilient, effective services that we have. Looking at our role as a regulator and in prevention.

Looking at stronger relationships and working with other agencies and communities. It is about making sure that we've got stronger business foundations, and it's about supporting our people to be effective through our business. Okay. So I've got a follow-up here. Yeah.

Mike Davidson. But to that, the fleet strategy, when was the decision to actually do a fleet strategy made? Well, there's been lots of discussion around a fleet strategy. And it goes right back even to the International Convention Center fire, where through there, there was a recommendation that we needed to have a fleet strategy in place.

The realization of actually developing a fleet strategy showed that we first needed to have things like the asset management plans, and we needed to have the future operating capability work that informs those to actually bring it all together. Otherwise, we're putting together a fleet strategy that won't effectively... It'll sit in a drawer and it won't be effective because it's not having the right injects in it to actually inform it to allow us to be successful in that.

Okay. We're going to Lamona on screen. Thanks, Madam Chair. Hopefully you can hear me. Yes, very good. And hopefully I'll continue to follow on. I would like to know from the explanation this morning and from the new board chair's opening words in terms of the strategy that is supposedly, and hopefully I've heard it properly, fit for purpose, because lots of the feedback that I've had as a member of parliament, but also from the community, is in terms of what is relevant and what is out of date.

And all of us around the select committee have had a number of concerns raised by many different various firefighters. We've visited fire stations. How relevant, in terms of the five-year strategy, will that be in terms of moving forward? So, appreciate your explanation to the CEO. So I'd like to hear from CEO, please.

Yeah, thank you. Appreciate the question. Of course, 90% of our appliances into the determined asset age. So I think that gives a really good way in which we're going to move the fleet forward.

Having that information and having that plan allows us to actually give effect to it now over the next few years. Supplementary, Madam Chair? Yes. Thank you for the replies. In terms of the workforce, I might be asking out of turn, Madam Chair. No, just ask it and I'll rule it in or out if I- Okay. Thank you. So in terms of the workforce, I want to ask questions around training and planning, and what is scheduled. We have had answers during the recent hearings, but I would like to ask, in terms of will the whole training and

development and workforce, will those sections of your overall plan, when do they come in? And how effective are they in terms of rolling out? So I've heard the questions that you've asked earlier. You've got a five-year window. How is that built into the current environment of firefighters and training and development?

Yeah. It's on the border of a fleet inquiry. But if you can bring it, if there's an answer that brings it into scope, or if you think it's out of scope, if there's anything that brings it in. Yeah, no, I'm happy to answer the question, and I think it is relevant as far as when we bring operational appliances on board, there's a training component that sits in there as- Yeah... ensuring that people understand the new technology and the new components and that. But if I talk about training itself, with a workforce of

14,000 people, and of those 11,800 roughly are volunteers, it does bring some unique challenges to training, in the training system, I guess, that we have as an organization. So, you will notice from the literature that one of the areas that we're reinvesting into, so that we're trying to create some space to reinvest in, is around training. And we've been doing a lot of good work around training, and even speaking with the committee last year when we looked at the work that we'd done to go back to a Category IV GTE around the

moderation and assessment work in our training. Lots of, I guess- bespoke improvements across training, but not looking at the training system as a whole. So the training system as a whole is going to be a multi-year program, because it's, I guess in a way similar to fleet, when foreign emergency came together, it brought different training environments and approaches from all the different entities that came in, and foreign emergencies never really looked at that as the system and saying, "What does our training system need

to look like?" And that's where our investment and time and energy's going in at the moment, and it's a focus of mine, it's a focus of the DCE responsible for that, and it's a focus of the board, which is why it's one of those areas of reinvestment for us as an organization. Thank you. Thank you. And next question's from Andy Foster.

Yeah, look, thank you. I'm just looking at, in terms of you're thinking about strategy, one of the things that you said to us that you don't know what the future's going to look like, and you then gave us an answer which talked about business foundations, supporting your people to be effective, relationships, and all sorts of other things like that. I didn't hear anything there at all about fleet, although I'm assuming that supporting our people to be effective, which was the words you used, I think- Mm... means you're actually going to have some fire engines that actually work for

people to do their work. In what possible scenario is there in future that you are not going to need the kind of fire engines that you're using at the moment? You're certainly going to need aerials. Mm-hmm. Probably more so than now, because if intensification continues.

You're certainly going to need your Type Threes, but you're going backwards at the moment. You've been going backwards since FENZ was established. Thank you, and if I look at the essence of your question, firstly, when I talk about stronger business foundations, that is about our fleet, and that is about how we build a fleet that actually supports our organization, supports our firefighters to do the phenomenal work that they do across the country every day.

What I would say in there is that, if you talk about the changing environment, and yes, I take your point around the current fleet that we have, is going to be required in the years to come, and that's why we've got a current focus on stabilizing the fleet that we've got. Our asset management plans with the 10-year plan will move the state of the fleet up. It will make a difference in there, and that's why we've developed that work.

But some of the things that need to be considered there, and I'll get Megan to talk about this in a minute, but you look at the role that foreign emergency plays in weather events at the moment for as an instance. You spoke about aerial appliances. What role does drones play in that? So there's a lot of questions that need to be answered as technology advances, as things go on, rather than just a status quo. But do you want to speak, Megan, just a little bit around some of the things you're seeing and considering as part of what our assets-

... and portfolio might look like? Yeah. Thanks, Kerry. When I first came to foreign emergency, it was evident that we had to, as Kerry has mentioned, stabilize our existing fleet because it was beyond the age that where we wanted it. Part of the work I'm really proud to lead on behalf of operational response is who do we need to be in the future, and that's what's coming out of the FOC work.

As firefighters, if we go back 20 years, we would never have thought our role would’ve been 45% motor vehicle and medical. So that shows you how quickly our industry changes. What the FOC, Future Operating Capability, is wanting to do is cast out about what could happen in our future, then bring it back into reasonable time frames.

So, for example, where will technology take us as firefighters in 10, 20 years? Then bring it back into a reasonable five year. What can we do over the next five years that progresses us towards that future? We have technology, we have the built environment, it is all created at a very fast pace, and for us to imagine what it's going to look like in 2040, we'd be aiming for something that mightn't exist.

So I think the five-year frames is reasonable. It gives us enough time to procure new fleet or equipment, and gives us enough time to also train our people appropriately for that capability that we see ahead. Great. So look, if I can just follow up with a sup there. You said 20 years ago that a lot of your, you wouldn't have considered that, what do you, I think you said 45% of your role medical, motor vehicle, et cetera?

Yes. But that doesn't mean that your firefighting role has diminished, that just means something else has been added on top of it. Which does go to the issue, which is not part of this inquiry, but does go to the issue of how FENZ is funded, which I'm very grateful the minister has actually taken that up. But the incidence of fire hasn't gone away, and I don't think you would be telling me it's diminished either.

No. You've still got to have vehicles that are fit for purpose to do that core part of your job. Yes. Thank you. And, I agree with you, and that is why our focus has been on stabilizing our core fleet. There will be potentially other demands on what are the capabilities that we need through that, but at the end of the day, our primary responsibility under the legislation sits in there around fire, and that will always be at the core of what we do. The size of the network and how that network distribution looks- is something that needs to be considered as far as what's the risk

profile of the different areas. There's a big difference between the risk profile in a really isolated rural community to that in the heart of a major city. So the type of appliances, the type of equipment isn't just a one-size-fits-all. I get that.

Yeah. I get that. But at the moment, when you talk about stabilizing your fleet, you are still going backwards because the rate at which you should be replacing the fleet to keep you under your age cap, you should be progressing forwards, but you've been going backwards essentially since FENZ started, certainly with the Type Threes and with the aerials. You're correct with Type Threes, certainly.

If you look at the graphs that we've provided in there across the Type Ones and Twos in the rural fleet, we've been holding the line in there. That's why I didn't include them. Yep. But with the Type Threes, like I said before, it has been very frustrating and the time that it's taken because of a number of reasons to actually get those Type Threes on the run, and procured and into New Zealand, has been a challenge for us as an organization.

Okay, thank you. I'll come back on those things later on. Okay, thanks, Andy. And I've got two more primaries in this section, the first being from Tim. Thank you. Just for the board chair, one of your goals you said at the start was about having greater board visibility. So in the initial hearing to this inquiry, I asked the then board chair if she and if the board had been asking questions about the Type Three man trucks, the same questions that we had been asking the last couple of years, and she emphatically told me yes, and that she was just as concerned as we were.

In the response to question 40 that I submitted after that hearing, where I asked for the reference from those board meetings, there are none after December 2023. So how do you explain that? Thank you for the question. As you would appreciate, it is very difficult for me to explain what happened previously. Firstly, because I haven't put my mind to it, and secondly, I wasn't there.

But I think the intention of your question, I can address that. It is my expectation that the organization, when we appear before Parliament, we provide information that is accurate, complete, and readily understandable. And if there's uncertainty, we will say so.

If the numbers change, we will explain why, and if we discover an error, we will correct it promptly. So I cannot speak for the past, but I want to give you assurance that the organization that I am chair of, my expectations will be very clear that when we tell this committee or anyone in Parliament that we have had a certain degree of oversight, we should be able to provide the evidence to prove that.

Yeah, but my fundamental question is, has the board had, the board that you now lead, I appreciate it wasn't you at the time, but have they had the appropriate level of oversight? Because we have not been given any evidence that suggests that for all of 2024 and all of 2025, this topic was even raised once. Yeah.

Thank you. What I'm saying is, I do not have an answer to that here now, but either the chief executive of the offices may have that, but we can always bring the information to you. Sure. And Kerry has his hand up, so I'm going to hand to him. Thank you, Chair. And, yeah, I just wanted to add into that conversation that the board has been holding us to account through their financial investment and sustainability committee, so the subcommittee of the board.

And that feeds up through to the minister's office has been having a lot of focus on us as an organization and what we're doing in fleet and the interest as part of those discussions that we have with her on a regular basis. But the main focus for the board has been through their FISC committee.

I understand that answer. The issue that we have is that it's a really clear question that has been submitted in writing. Can the board please share minutes of meetings where they have asked FENZ staff about tranche two man Type Three appliances? And there are quite a few between 2017 and 2023. There's nothing beyond that.

And this is the only tool that the public have for oversight, is the board. And I think there is a genuine concern out there as to whether or not they've been doing their function. Does the board have the right people, the right capability, the right skills and experience to actually fulfill the role that they hold? What would your view as the chair be? Well, thank you. As Chair, I would say that I agree that the board needs to have the appropriate skills to function and to provide that rigorous oversight on assurance, accountability, and execution.

Do you currently have that? I would not know, and so it would be improper for me to provide a judgment at this stage. Thank you. We've got one more question in this section, and so we're coming to the end, so I'll hand over to Mike. Yeah, thank you. And I've just got a couple of little subs to follow on from- Yeah... Beth Foster. And I guess it was the comment you made around holding the line with your, I guess the initial nine years around the oil and other appliances apart from Type 3. Was that a directive to hold the line over that period of time, or were you actually meant

to improve the standard of the fleet? Well, certainly, if you look at the Type 3s, the intention of the Type 3s was to procure- Oh, sorry, I'm not talking about the Type 3s. You were saying the other appliances, you're holding the line. Mm-hmm. You've held the line.

Yeah. Was that a directive to hold the line and just actually keep it at the state they were in, or you meant to actually improve the standard of the fleet? Well, the aspiration is always to improve it. But, we are balancing the fleet across all of the asset classes and the prioritization across those asset classes.

And we've- I guess I'm wondering, I looked at, and you mentioned in the submission that you've invested 114 million over the last nine years. Mm. And if you look at your total revenue you've received over that nine years, it's circa 6.3 billion, so this equates to 1.8%.

Mm. Do you think that was enough to be going into the fleet during the last nine years? Especially when you look forward and you're budgeting 356 million over the next 10 years and saying that's 154 million short. Mm. Do you think you were budgeting enough over the last nine years- Mm... to actually move forward in the right direction?

I'll pass to Gerald to fill in around the allocation of the different finances in the different areas. But what I would say is that, what we've been balancing there is investment in the right parts of the organization to keep moving it forward. And, if we'd invested more into the fleet, the question of that is, where does it fall over somewhere else?

So, in balancing and the fiscal parameters that we have, making the right decisions, I think the balancing across the fleet, has led us to the situation we are. And whether that could've been different- So do you think the fact we're here today means that it wasn't balanced correctly? Well, do you want to talk about how we've balanced that, Gerald, across the different areas?

It's a simple question. Mm. How it was balanced in the past to basically put 1.8% of the total revenue towards fleet, do you think that was the right call in hindsight? I think that the reason that we are here today is predominantly because of the challenges that we've had around the Type 3 fleet, and that doesn't necessarily come into the investment in there.

It comes into some of the challenges and issues we've had being able to find the right solution and get that put in place. So yes, I do think that the balance across the asset portfolio has been right. So you're saying if we didn't have the issues with the Type 3, you wouldn't be sitting at this end of the table right now? We'd obviously still be reporting to select committee, but I don't think we'd be having the same discussions today that we would be having.

Okay. I think I've got it primarily now. We were hoping that we'd see the national fleet manager today, but our understanding is he's resigned and left, which I guess was a bit of a surprise at the time. Did he give his required contracted notice period before he left?

Certainly, the national manager left and we were comfortable with the notice that he gave us as an organization. And there was- Was it the same as the contracted notice period? I don't know that information. I'd have to have a look at what his particular contract was with us in that regard.

Did he receive an exit package that would be greater than just his holiday pay?
